source.title: Problems in Data Structures and Algorithms

accepted.question_text: Let Σ be a finite alphabet, and suppose strings over Σ are generated from an initially empty stack by three operations: push(A), which pushes a letter A onto the stack; emit, which outputs the current top letter; and pop, which removes the current top letter. The operation sequence must be well formed: it starts and ends with an empty stack and never pops an empty stack. Given a target string σ over Σ, what is the best possible running time for computing a minimum-length sequence of stack operations that generates σ? In particular, can this optimization problem be solved in O(n^2) time or even O(n log n) time for input length n, and what upper or lower bounds can be proved?

evidence.quote: We are given a finite alphabet Σ, and a stack S. We would like to generate strings of letters over the alphabet using the stack. There are three stack operations we can perform. push (A)—push the letter A from the alphabet onto the stack, emit—output the top letter from the stack, pop—pop the top letter from the stack.
Problem 2.1 Given some string σ over the alphabet, find a minimum length sequence of stack operations to generate σ.

I have no idea whether the problem can be solved in O(n2) or in O(n log n) time. Solving this problem, or getting a better upper bound, or a better lower bound, would reveal more information about context-free parsing than what we currently know.

accepted.question_text: Consider the online splaying algorithm for binary search trees: after each access, the accessed item is moved to the root by a sequence of rotations, with each rotation costing one unit, and the access cost itself is the number of nodes on the search path from the root to the item. For every initial binary search tree on n items and every access sequence, is the total cost of splaying always within a constant factor of the minimum total cost achievable by an optimal offline algorithm that knows the entire access sequence in advance and may choose any pattern of rotations?

evidence.quote: Problem 4.4 Dynamic Optimality Conjecture: Prove or disprove that for any initial tree and any access sequence, the splaying algorithm comes within a constant factor of the optimal off-line algorithm.

Suppose we begin with some n-node search tree and perform a sequence of accesses. (For simplicity, we ignore insertions and deletions.) The cost to access an item is the number of nodes on the path from the root to the item. At any time, we can perform one or more rotations, at a cost of one per rotation. Then, knowing the entire access sequence ahead of time, there is a pattern of rotations that minimizes the total cost of the accesses and the rotations. This is the optimal offline algorithm, for the given initial tree and the given access sequence.

accepted.question_text: For binary search tree access sequences, does there exist any online update algorithm—not necessarily splaying—whose total cost is always within a constant factor of the optimum offline algorithm that knows the full future access sequence in advance?

evidence.quote: A weaker form of Problem 4.4 asks whether there is any on-line algorithm whose performance is within a constant factor of that of the optimum off-line algorithm.

accepted.question_text: Even if the full dynamic optimality conjecture remains open, can one prove that splaying achieves a log log competitive bound against the optimal offline binary-search-tree algorithm, analogous to the log log performance factor obtained by Demaine and collaborators for a different online search-tree update algorithm?

evidence.quote: They have designed an on-line search tree update algorithm that comes within a loglog performance factor of the optimal off-line algorithm (as compared to the log factor of a balanced tree algorithm).
An immediate question is whether one can prove a similar loglog bound for splaying, even if the dynamic optimality conjecture remains out of reach.

accepted.question_text: Given two binary search trees with the same n ordered keys, determine the minimum number of rotations needed to transform one tree into the other. In particular, is there an efficient algorithm for computing this rotation distance exactly, or is the problem computationally intractable?

evidence.quote: Problem 5.1 Given two n-node trees, how many rotations does it take to convert one tree into the other?
This question seems to be NP- hard.

accepted.question_text: Let w1, w2, ..., wn be positive weights on n ordered items, and consider binary search trees that store the items in their internal nodes, with the i-th item appearing in symmetric order at depth di. What is the fastest algorithm for constructing a tree minimizing Σ_i w_i d_i? In particular, can the classical O(n^2) dynamic-programming bound be improved, and can any nontrivial lower bound be proved for this optimization problem?
accepted.context_brief: static optimal BST with internal nodes

evidence.quote: Problem 6.1 Items can be stored in the internal nodes of the tree. ... Given positive weights w1, w2,...,wn, construct an n-node binary tree that minimizes n i=1 widi , where di is the depth of the i-th node in symmetric order.

Here we have an O(n2) dynamic programming algorithm with a certain amount of cleverness in it. This result is twenty-five years old or so. Nothing better is known. There may, in fact, be a faster algorithm for Problem 6.1; no nontrivial lower bound for the problem is known.

accepted.question_text: Let w1, w2, ..., wn be positive weights on n ordered items, and consider alphabetic binary search trees in which the items may appear only in the external nodes (leaves), with the i-th external node at depth di in symmetric order. What is the true complexity of constructing a tree minimizing Σ_i w_i d_i? In particular, can this problem be solved in linear time, or can one prove a lower bound ruling that out?

evidence.quote: Problem 6.2 Items can be stored only in the external nodes (the leaves) of the tree. The problem in this case is: Given positive weights w1, w2,...,wn, construct a binary tree with n external nodes that minimizes n i=1 widi , where di is the depth of the i-th external node in symmetric order.

And again, there is no lower bound known. In fact, there is no reason to believe that the problem cannot be solved in linear time, and there is good reason to believe that maybe it can: for some interesting special cases the problem can indeed be solved in linear time [27].

accepted.question_text: For the minimum spanning tree problem in a connected undirected graph with m edges and n vertices, is random sampling actually necessary in order to obtain linear running time? Equivalently, does there exist a deterministic linear-time algorithm for computing a minimum spanning tree?

evidence.quote: One may ask whether random sampling is really necessary. Is there a deterministic linear-time algorithm to find minimum spanning trees?

In conclusion, we now know that minimum spanning trees can be found in linear time using random sampling, and we know an optimum deterministic algorithm but we don’t know how fast it runs (no slower than O(m α(n)), possibly as fast as O(m)).
